text: The Rent shall be paid monthly in advance.
All other repairs are to be carried out by the Lessee.
The premises may be used only as offices.
The lease may be terminated by the other party.
The rent shall be paid by the fifth business day.
The deposit is to be paid on signature.
The lease may be terminated if the breach is not remedied.
Structural repairs are to be carried out by the owner.
It says it shall be done, but by whom?

I've been renting out apartments in Chicago for fifteen years, and the conversation I have most often is about the deposit. When a tenant moves out, they expect every cent back. When I look at the apartment, I see a list of repairs. The truth is usually somewhere in the middle. Normal wear and tear is my problem: faded paint, a carpet that has been walked on for three years, a door handle that has gotten loose. That is simply what happens when people live somewhere. Damage is different. A hole in the wall, a broken window, a burn on the kitchen counter: those are paid for by the tenant, and that money comes out of the deposit. My advice to anybody who rents is very simple. On the first day, walk through every room with your phone and take pictures of everything. Then send them to the landlord by email, so the date is recorded. Three years later, when we disagree about a scratch on the floor, those pictures will be worth more than any clause in the lease.

I have been drafting contracts for twenty-five years, and I still spend more time on one small word than on any other: shall. In a well-drafted contract, shall means one thing only: this party has a duty. The tenant shall pay the rent. The trouble starts when lawyers use the passive and forget to say who owes the duty. The premises shall be kept in good condition. By whom? The landlord, or the tenant? I once saw a dispute about a broken elevator last two years because of a sentence like that. So my rule is simple. Whenever you write a passive sentence in a contract, ask yourself whether the reader knows who has to act. If the answer is not obvious, add by and the name of the party, or rewrite the sentence in the active voice. The passive is not the enemy. It is useful when the action matters more than the person. But in a list of obligations, an obligation without an owner is an argument waiting to happen.
The rent shall be paid by the fifth business day.
The deposit is to be paid on signature.
Structural repairs are to be carried out by the owner.
The owner is liable for repairs to the roof.
Faded paint is normal wear and tear.
They have thirty days to remedy the breach.
The lease may be terminated if the breach is not remedied.
It says it shall be done, but by whom?
